Path tie-breaking remains deterministic since k is always the outer loop regardless of inner parallelization, and I'm now considering overflow bounds given INF=1e9 and edge weights up to 200 across n nodes.\n\nGiven the problem is a complete graph with weights 1-200, all distances stay finite so INF never actually appears, which simplifies the arithmetic.\n\nNow I'm thinking about the hybrid MPI/OpenMP/CUDA design: rows get distributed across MPI ranks, with OpenMP and CUDA handling intra-rank parallelism. I also want to check the results_output.hpp header to confirm how print_results_int formats its output so I preserve identical formatting in my implementation.\n\nFor the distributed Floyd-Warshall algorithm, I'm settling on a row-block decomposition: each rank owns a contiguous range of rows, and for each iteration k, the owning rank broadcasts pivot row k to everyone else via MPI_Bcast. Since the diagonal is always zero, row k never changes during its own iteration, so the broadcast can happen safely at the start of each iteration without any race condition.\n\nFor performance, I'm considering whether compute dominates over communication for large n, which it does, so a simple blocking broadcast per iteration is reasonable rather than attempting complex pipelining with async broadcasts. {"type":"tool_use","timestamp":1793046333698,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"type":"tool","tool":"write","callID":"toolu_014qHfCmJQg5ez44ouBBhSB2","state":{"status":"completed","input":{"filePath":"/home/llmtest/evals/20261025-170040/floydwarshall_claude-haiku-5.5-oc-medium_hybrid_r3/floydwarshall/floydwarshall.cpp","content":"#include <mpi.h>\n#include <omp.h>\n#include <cuda_runtime.h>\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstdlib>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include \"../common/results_output.hpp\"\n\nconstexpr unsigned int INF = 1000000000;\nconstexpr unsigned int MAX_DISTANCE = 200;\n\n// Fraction of each rank's rows updated on its GPU. The remaining rows are\n// updated concurrently by OpenMP host threads of the same rank.\nconstexpr double GPU_ROW_FRACTION = 0.85;\n\n#define CUDA_CHECK(call)                                                          \\\n    do {                                                                          \\\n        cudaError_t err_ = (call);                                                \\\n        if (err_ != cudaSuccess) {                                                \\\n            fprintf(stderr, \"CUDA error at %s:%d: %s\\n\", __FILE__, __LINE__,     \\\n                    cudaGetErrorString(err_));                                    \\\n            MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1);                                         \\\n        }                                                                         \\\n    } while (0)\n\n// Index calculation for flattened 2D array\ninline constexpr size_t idx2(const size_t i, const size_t j, const size_t n) noexcept {\n    return j * n + i;\n}\n\n// First row owned by `rank` in a block-row distribution of n rows over `size` ranks.\nstatic size_t rowStart(const size_t n, const int rank, const int size) {\n    return n * static_cast<size_t>(rank) / static_cast<size_t>(size);\n}\n\n// Generates the full random matrix in the same sequence as the original code,\n// but stores only the rows [r0, r1) owned by this rank.\nvoid initializeDistanceRows(std::vector<unsigned int>& local, const size_t numNodes,\n                            const size_t r0, const size_t r1,\n                            const unsigned int rangeMin, const unsigned int rangeMax) {\n    unsigned int seed = 42;\n    const double range = static_cast<double>(rangeMax - rangeMin) + 1.0;\n\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < numNodes; ++i) {\n        const bool owned = (i >= r0 && i < r1);\n        unsigned int* row = owned ? {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793046733240,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"id":"prt_179e9c19b001EZnYEz7sPHiKhV","messageID":"msg_179e9bc42001eZ2Osnte513gyj","sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","type":"reasoning","text":"Interesting result: at frac=1.0 with threads=1, it's pure GPU work at 544ms, but with threads=64 it jumps to 4424ms even though there's no CPU rows to process. That suggests the overhead comes from spinning up the empty OpenMP parallel region itself on every step, not from actual work.\n\nThe real culprit is likely 64 idle OMP threads spin-waiting (GOMP spin policy) competing for cores with CUDA's own busy-wait during stream synchronization—oversubscription causing contention. A simple fix would be skipping the parallel region entirely when there are zero CPU rows. Looking at the frac=0.85 case, the per-step cost of synchronizing GPU and CPU work is heavy: at 1 thread the CPU chunk processes roughly 2.5M row updates per step in about 1ms, which is actually quite fast for a single AVX2 thread, but scaling to 64 threads makes things slower rather than faster, pointing to synchronization/barrier overhead dominating over any parallel speedup.\n\nThe GPU side handles 14M updates in about 0.13ms per step, so the slowdown isn't on that end. It's possible the CPU threads are spinning rather than blocking during the GPU sync, which could explain the contention — I should try OMP_WAIT_POLICY=passive and test cudaDeviceScheduleBlockingSync to see if that resolves the overhead.\n\n","time":{"start":1793046725019,"end":1793046733206},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793046882127,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"id":"prt_179ebec26001S8lXSFxuK0KvQH","messageID":"msg_179ebe6480013NnZ60C3ww8M7q","sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","type":"reasoning","text":"The GPU-only runtime of 544ms is consistent across runs, but adding CPU work with 8 threads balloons total time to about 4 seconds, showing host-side work is far slower per unit than GPU work. Checking the numbers at 0.85 fraction, 1 thread gives roughly the same ~4s, suggesting the CPU portion's cost dominates almost independent of thread count, which points to a bottleneck elsewhere.\n\nThat's odd since parallelism should cut per-thread time at 8 threads, yet the measured per-step time stays near 1ms regardless. So I'm now questioning whether something like OMP thread-team setup overhead or another serialization point is masking the expected speedup, and I'm cross-checking against the frac=0 case with 64 threads to estimate per-thread throughput and see if the numbers are consistent with a single shared bottleneck.\n\nChecking the math against memory bandwidth, this looks like a NUMA first-touch problem — the vector gets allocated and zero-initialized on the main thread's node, so all 64 threads end up contending for one NUMA node's bandwidth (~40GB/s), and the bytes-moved-per-step calculations line up closely with the observed timings for both the dense and sparse fraction cases. The fix would be to re-touch the memory in parallel with OpenMP so pages get distributed across NUMA nodes matching thread affinity.\n\nSeparately, I'm weighing whether it's even worth optimizing the CPU path further: comparing CPU bandwidth (~16-40GB/s) against GPU bandwidth (~936GB/s), the CPU's useful contribution to a combined GPU+CPU scheme is only a couple percent, so the synchronization complexity may not be worth it — maybe OpenMP is better spent on pivot-independent work, initialization, or post-processing instead of trying to squeeze out marginal speedup from the hybrid compute.\n\nAt multi-GPU scale, each step's GPU work becomes so short (tens of microseconds) that OpenMP fork/join overhead starts to dominate, making the hybrid CPU contribution actively harmful for scaling rather than helpful. I'm now considering better uses for OpenMP: it's probably not worth it for the hot loop, but it could genuinely help with serial initialization work like random number generation, which otherwise wastes time with no parallelism at all.\n\nI'm testing whether NUMA-aware memory placement with thread pinning could make the CPU share actually competitive with the GPU—if the CPU could hit 100+ GB/s with proper first-touch allocation across 64 threads, that's comparable to the GPU's ~126 GB/s, which would justify a much larger CPU work fraction. Running a streaming benchmark to check achievable bandwidth with this setup.\n\nThe results show the bandwidth isn't limited the way I expected since the test data fits inside the EPYC's massive 256MB L3 cache rather than hitting main memory, so that benchmark doesn't really reflect the real matrix workload behavior. Rather than keep speculating, I should just directly profile the CPU-only case across various thread counts and compare per-step timing against the actual GPU/CPU split numbers I already have.\n\n","time":{"start":1793046866982,"end":1793046882115},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"step_start","timestamp":1793047051777,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"id":"prt_179eebdfa001iDXMLgV81x1BTI","messageID":"msg_179eeb7590011clRrBGzgdtRCx","sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","type":"step-start"}}
{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793047096123,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"id":"prt_179eebdfd001LYhOLGSZB7fWLx","messageID":"msg_179eeb7590011clRrBGzgdtRCx","sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm noticing the throughput numbers don't line up cleanly: np=4 stays around 290ms regardless of fraction, suggesting GPU-bound behavior near 240 G/s total across 4 GPUs (60 G/s each), while np=1 on a single GPU shows 544ms implying roughly 126 G/s—oddly higher per-GPU than the multi-GPU case, which seems inconsistent and worth digging into further.\n\nThe real culprit looks like per-step fixed latency rather than compute: with 4096 steps at ~70us each that's the 290ms for np=4, pointing to MPI_Bcast overhead plus the D2H/H2D pivot-row synchronization chain rather than linear scaling. I'm weighing fixes—avoiding the D2H-sync-Bcast-H2D chain via async pipelining (complex), CUDA-aware MPI (uncertain availability), or blocking multiple k-steps together to cut synchronization frequency by a factor of B, which seems like the most promising real fix despite added complexity.\n\nSo the ~70us figure is really fixed per-step latency: D2H, host sync, Bcast across ranks, H2D, kernel launch, and sync overhead dominate rather than raw compute. Comparing to np=1 where per-step time is ~133us almost entirely kernel work, it seems at np=4 the kernel itself only takes ~33us but gets swallowed by that fixed communication/sync latency.\n\nTo cut this, I'm considering CUDA-aware MPI to skip the D2H/H2D round trip, or better, pipelining: compute the next pivot row early in its own small kernel, async copy it to pinned host memory, and issue an MPI_Ibcast so non-owner ranks can keep working on the current step's kernel while waiting for the broadcast to land, only blocking before launching the next step. This would need double-buffered pivot storage to overlap steps cleanly.\n\nI'm working out the synchronization ordering: the owner must finish computing just the pivot row before triggering the D2H copy and Ibcast, which means splitting the owner's kernel into a tiny one-row launch followed by the rest, using a CUDA event to signal row completion without a full stream sync, then having the host wait on that event before posting the broadcast while the remaining rows continue computing concurrently.\n\nI'm weighing whether the complexity is worth it — overlapping the broadcast with kernel work might cut per-step latency roughly in half for small n at np=4, but for large n the kernel time dominates so the gain shrinks. A simpler, higher-impact alternative might be blocked Floyd-Warshall with block size B, which reduces kernel launches and syncs by a factor of B but requires broadcasting B pivot rows every B steps and sequentially handling the in-block dependencies on the owner.\n\nSo pivot row k at step k equals the true row state after applying steps k0 through k-1, meaning the owner just computes those B rows fully sequentially within itself before broadcasting.\n\nFor all other rows, I process them against the sequential pivot updates: dist[i][j] at step k depends on dist[i][k] and the pivot row's value at that same step, since the broadcasted pivot row must reflect its state at step k, not after the full block. I need to check whether row k itself gets mutated by later steps within the same block.\n\nFor each non-block row, I'm fusing the B rank-1 updates into one pass over the row, where at each step the pivot column value comes from the row's own current state before being combined with the snapshot.\n\nI'm realizing the block-column values themselves get updated sequentially within the same block, so each thread needs to recompute those intermediate column states as a per-row prefix process, with every thread in the row redundantly deriving the same sequence of updates rather than relying on a separate pass.\n\nI'm working out that one thread per (row, column) element can persist across all B steps within a tile, reading the pivot value from shared memory after it's written by the owning column's thread at the prior step, then updating its own distance with a min-plus operation against the pivot row buffer, and syncing threads between each step so writes and reads don't race.\n\nWith two syncs per step, this batching reduces memory traffic by roughly B since there's one global read/write per element per block of B steps instead of per single step, and pivot values can live in smem or L2 cache affordably. For GPU/MPI, broadcasting B rows per block instead of one also cuts synchronization overhead by that same factor.\n\nThe owner computing its B pivot snapshots is trickier since it's inherently sequential and block rows may span multiple owners at partition boundaries unless I force alignment to B, which adds complexity. Given the time budget, I think the current design is correct and reasonably efficient, and further optimization would require substantial additional engineering.\n\nStill, since the user wants maximum performance, I'm trying to estimate the potential gains from blocking: with B=32, memory traffic drops roughly 32x and the kernel becomes compute-bound rather than overhead-bound, which could meaningfully cut the current ~290ms runtime on n=4096 across 4 GPUs by reducing the dominant overhead component.\n\nI'm weighing whether there's a middle ground that keeps the per-k structure but reduces synchronization frequency, versus moving to a fully blocked 3-phase Floyd-Warshall with proper row ownership alignment for the pivot blocks, which is more complex with MPI row distribution but could yield the biggest speedup.\n\nSince those block rows only depend on prior completed steps plus other block rows, once the owners have the correct state up to k0, I just need the B rows gathered at the start of the block—one batched broadcast of B×n data rather than B separate broadcasts, even if the rows come from different owners.\n\nEach rank then redundantly recomputes the in-block closure over B rows, which is cheap relative to the full n²/P cost — but I need to check whether this is fast enough on GPU vs CPU: for n=4096, B=32 it's around 0.5G ops per rank, too slow on CPU but feasible on GPU at roughly 40ms total across all blocks, though that overhead is still non-trivial.\n\nThis is turning into a major rewrite requiring hours of careful work, so given the constraints I'll stop optimizing the blocked algorithm and keep the current per-k design, acknowledging honestly that the synchronous per-step chain limits multi-GPU scaling and that a blocked Floyd-Warshall would be the natural next step. Since the OpenMP CPU share isn't actually contributing meaningfully at np=4 (and even hurts at np=1), I'm considering whether there's a cheap way to make it useful without harm, possibly by overlapping the synchronization chain with ongoing kernel work.\n\nI'm sketching a pipelining approach: at each step k, after broadcasting pivot row k and launching the kernel for all local rows, the owner of row k+1 would compute that row early via a dedicated small kernel, copy it back asynchronously on a separate stream, then broadcast it while the main kernel for step k continues running concurrently for everyone else — though I need to check whether applying the rank-1 min-update twice to that row (once in the early kernel, once again in the full step-k kernel) causes correctness issues since the operation isn't strictly idempotent.\n\nI convince myself it is idempotent here, since reapplying the same minimum-with-pivot update a second time produces no change — so I can just split kernel_k into two launches, one excluding row k+1, to keep the owner's special row from being double-counted. This overlap should hide the broadcast latency behind the kernel execution, cutting per-step chain time roughly in half, though it depends on OpenMPI actually making progress on the non-blocking broadcast while other ranks wait.\n\nStepping back, I realize this optimization only matters much for small-n cases at low process counts, since at large n the kernel's memory traffic dominates — though my quick back-of-envelope bandwidth estimate for n=4096 doesn't add up, so I want to just gather real numbers. I decide to test n=8192 with np=1 versus np=4 to see how well it scales at larger problem sizes, where per-step communication overhead should matter much less.\n\n","time":{"start":1793047051773,"end":1793047096063},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793047176826,"sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","part":{"id":"prt_179efd743001cnNnIkXAL5KaYe","messageID":"msg_179efd153001EJtvGMf9IWnLnu","sessionID":"ses_e861ebec7fferQN1o03rDJw3Tz","type":"reasoning","text":"At n=8192, single GPU hits 159 G/s while four GPUs reach 392 G/s—only 2.5x scaling, suggesting there's blocked bandwidth limiting further gains, with maybe 5-10x headroom. I'm weighing which single improvement would give the best payoff for the risk involved.\n\nBlocked kernels with register accumulation need block pivot logic, which gets messy with the MPI row distribution since it requires tracking pivot snapshots across blocks. A cheaper alternative is cutting memory traffic, but the math shows the per-k kernel is already near bandwidth-bound—roughly 0.64 TB/s of effective throughput against a 936GB/s ceiling—so blocking really is the only path to a major speedup, which points me toward trying shared-memory tiling in the per-k kernel.\n\nFor a blocked approach, the in-block dependency means rows k0..k1-1 must be processed sequentially, so I'd gather that B-row block to all ranks via broadcasts and have each rank redundantly compute the in-block closure itself. For B=64 and n=8192 this costs about 33M ops per rank per block, totaling roughly 4.3G ops across 128 blocks—manageable as a small sequential-in-k kernel updating 524k elements per step.\n\nI'm estimating this closure overhead relative to the main n³/P work: the ratio comes out to about BP/n ≈ 3%, which is cheap enough to be worthwhile. The closure needs to snapshot each pivot row's state at its own step k (storing these into a B×n buffer) so they can later be applied to all other rows outside the block in a second phase that sequentially folds in the block's updates.\n\nFor that second phase, I'm designing a fused kernel where each thread owns one column element of a row and uses shared memory exchange between threads to get the current pivot-column value at each step, updating its own distance and path pointer if a shorter path through the pivot is found — needing two syncthreads per step, which is cheap.\n\nThe path register only needs writing once per block rather than per step, which reduces memory traffic, and since the pivot row P values are read-shared across threads they stay cached. Overall this should become compute-bound for block sizes around 32-64, trading off reduced global memory traffic against more arithmetic per thread.\n\nFor the CPU side, the in-place sequential update naturally gives exact semantics without needing separate buffers, since each row's block iteration just reads and writes directly into the same row array—simple and easy to vectorize. For the GPU, I'm considering a row-per-block alternative where an entire row fits into shared memory (32KB for n=8192), letting each block stage and update a row locally before writing back.\n\nSince each pivot-row update depends on the prior step's result at that same index, I need one `__syncthreads()` per step; storing both path and distance rows would need 64KB, which exceeds the default 48KB smem limit, though dynamic smem allocation up to ~99KB on sm_86 could work. Instead, I'm sketching a tiled kernel design: blocks of 32×8 threads, where each thread handles multiple columns (via an unroll factor J) and a subset of rows, to balance register use and shared memory smarter than a full-row-per-block scheme.\n\nWriting exchange buffer logic...\n\nEach step involves one global load of P (hitting L2), some shared-memory operations, and two syncs across 256 threads, which puts throughput somewhere around 10-20 G updates/s — though I suspect that estimate may be too optimistic.\n\nI'm realizing this sync-per-step approach is actually slower than the current 159 G/s baseline since it's latency-bound; I need to pack more work between syncs. Trying register tiling with multiple rows per thread (R=4) still leaves too many syncs relative to work done, so I'm considering a warp-level approach where each warp owns complete rows to avoid cross-warp synchronization entirely.\n\nIf B=32 columns align exactly to a warp's 32 lanes, then a block of columns lives entirely in one register slot per lane, letting me use `__shfl_sync`/`__syncwarp` instead of block-wide syncs — this alignment trick seems like the key to cutting sync overhead.\n\nGiven how much time I've already invested, I need to weigh whether pursuing the full blocked FW rewrite is worth the bug risk versus settling on the current design with a small tweak to avoid the CPU hybrid share hurting performance, since the data suggests host participation is actually detrimental.\n\nTesting a high GPU fraction like 0.9-0.95 to keep OpenMP nominally active without hurting throughput reveals something odd: at single-thread CPU runs, even a small 5% row share costs 3x slowdown, because per-thread CPU throughput is only ~2.5 G/s, well below GPU's. Oddly, measurements show no real scaling with more threads, which is suspicious and worth probing further on this shared machine.\n\nChecking a cleaner baseline (frac=0, t=4 vs t=1) confirms the same lack of scaling, while a simple in-cache OpenMP test scaled fine from 47ms to 5ms with 16 threads — so the issue is specific to FW's memory access pattern. The 2048×2048 matrices (32MB working set) exceed per-CCX L3 cache, making each step memory-bound streaming from DRAM; computing the implied bandwidth (~40 GB/s for a single thread) seems way too high for one core, suggesting other tenants or shared memory bandwidth on this machine could be throttling things.\n\nGiven the load average of 50, this machine likely has heavy co-tenancy contesting memory bandwidth, meaning I can't reliably evaluate CPU scaling here — a dedicated node might show real speedup. I'm leaning toward keeping a hybrid CPU/GPU split with a modest, documented, tunable share rather than going full GPU-only, since the data suggests CPU share is roughly neutral around 10%. I also consider whether conditional stores could reduce memory traffic in later steps, but vectorizing that requires AVX-512 masked stores (not available on AVX2), so it's not worth the complexity — I'll finalize the fraction based on the flat results across 0.85–1.0 at np=4.\n\nBut I realize a static fraction can't generalize across different single-GPU vs multi-GPU setups: at np=1, a hybrid split would actually lose to GPU-only, yet at np=4 OpenMP needs to stay active to satisfy the \"use OpenMP as appropriate\" requirement. A proper fix would be runtime auto-calibration — measuring GPU and CPU step times early on and dynamically rebalancing the split — though that adds real complexity I need to weigh against just picking a reasonable static default.\n\nSo instead I'll redirect OpenMP toward host-side work that's always useful and never a hazard: pivot staging, initialization, and gather operations, which gives a trivial but legitimate gain regardless of split. For the actual row split, I'm leaning toward a self-calibrating approach: run the first several real Floyd-Warshall steps on both CPU and GPU paths against the actual data, measure the achieved throughput ratio, and use that to set the GPU row fraction proportionally — since those initial steps are genuine computation, this calibration doesn't corrupt correctness while adapting cleanly to whatever hardware it's running on.\n\nSince the device holds a contiguous prefix of rows, rebalancing after calibration is just a straightforward memcpy — moving rows from host to device if the GPU share should grow, or back if it should shrink. I'd allocate the device buffer at full local size upfront so the boundary can shift either way without reallocation, accepting the extra memory cost as a reasonable tradeoff for flexibility on modern GPU memory capacities.\n\nDuring calibration, I'd time CPU wall-clock loops and GPU kernel time separately using CUDA events, then compute each device's effective rows-per-second rate to set the split point g = localRows × rate_gpu/(rate_gpu+rate_cpu). Each rank would calibrate independently and rebalance its own prefix boundary, which should work fine approximately even though ranks stay loosely in lockstep via the broadcast each step. This seems like a modest, self-contained addition — maybe 60 lines — with the calibration window needing some fixed number of early steps to establish stable rate estimates.\n\nIf CPU throughput is poor, the split naturally shifts toward the GPU handling everything, so the scheme self-adapts without a hand-tuned constant; the cost is a few slower steps during calibration, negligible for a window of 8 or so. I'm now thinking through implementation details: allocating device buffers sized to the local row capacity, choosing an initial 50/50 split between GPU and CPU rows for the calibration phase, uploading that initial GPU chunk, and iterating through the calibration window.\n\nWithin each calibration step I'm timing GPU work with CUDA events and CPU work with wall-clock timing, accumulating totals only when each side actually has rows to process. At the end of the window I compute throughput rates for each side and use them to rebalance the row split proportionally, while handling edge cases like a localRows count too small to produce a meaningful GPU measurement -- in which case I just keep the initial split rather than attempting to rebalance from zero data.\n\nFor tiny row counts I set the initial split so GPU always gets at least one row, clamping the final split to stay within valid bounds so GPU is never starved entirely. The rebalance itself works by moving rows between host and device: growing the GPU's share means uploading the newly assigned host rows, shrinking it means downloading rows back to host, keeping the device array as a simple prefix of the local rows so indexing stays consistent.\n\nI'm also thinking through timing: using CUDA events only during the calibration window to avoid overhead elsewhere, picking a window size around 16 steps, and skipping the very first step since it's skewed by warmup costs like context creation and the first kernel launch. Rebalancing then happens once right after the calibration window closes, with small problem sizes simply skipping rebalancing altogether since there aren't enough steps to calibrate.\n\nSince the broadcast keeps ranks roughly in lockstep and all ranks rebalance at the same step boundary, the per-rank calibration stays consistent across the cluster even though each rank measures its own timing independently.\n\nNow I'm restructuring the main loop to split local rows between GPU and host threads, allocating device capacity for the maximum possible row count, and writing a helper to adjust how many rows the GPU handles when rebalancing kicks in.\n\nWriting memcpy rebalance logic...\n\nNow I'm adding CUDA event timers around the pivot copy and kernel execution, gated to only run during the calibration window, while separately timing the host-side forward step so I can compare GPU versus CPU throughput per step.\n\nAfter accumulating gpuMs and cpuMs over the calibration window, I compute throughput rates for each side and solve for the target GPU row count that balances the two, clamping it to stay within valid bounds and only triggering a rebalance when both sides actually have measurements to compare.\n\nNow I'll edit the source file: replacing the old GPU_ROW_FRACTION constant with the new kCalibSteps constant, adjusting the row computation, device allocation, and the calibration loop plus post-loop rebalance logic to match.\n\n","time":{"start":1793047123779,"end":1793047176801},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
